method: Reuses the full 510-item model/editorial review in docs/review/2026-11-18-japanese-usage-audit.md; current forms and actual distractors rebound to baseline 066ce2b. This is not a second independent native review.

findings.suggestion: こんにちは for a neutral daytime hello; retain やあ only as a labelled casual alternative.
findings.reason: Valid casual greeting, but not the requested neutral beginner default. こんにちは already occurs at 0269; allow legitimate shared translations and recheck actual distractors rather than inventing a rare synonym.

findings.suggestion: Keep さようなら for a suitable farewell context; use じゃあ、また with familiar people seen regularly, or a context-appropriate polite departure.
findings.reason: Not universally wrong, but not the everyday goodbye for every encounter. Japan Foundation explains farewell choices by relationship and situation.

findings.suggestion: Keep ありがとう as familiar thanks; consider ありがとうございます for polite stranger-facing use.
findings.reason: Register decision, not a mistranslation. A beginner default needs its intended addressee made explicit.

findings.suggestion: Replace 足 (0135) as a distractor for leg or provide an excluding context.
findings.reason: Actual English→Japanese leg question offers 脚 and 足. 足 can mean leg as well as foot, so distinct strings do not guarantee one defensible answer. Evidence reused from the prior review, which retrieved a search excerpt.

findings.suggestion: Replace 語句 (0403) as the distractor for word, or clearly separate the intended phrase sense.
findings.reason: 語句 can mean words and phrases. Actual English→Japanese choices include 単語 and 語句. Evidence reused from prior dictionary search excerpts.

findings.suggestion: Choose older/younger and own/other-family context before any rewrite.
findings.reason: Current wording literally says older or younger sister, preserving an underspecified meaning but functioning as an explanatory gloss rather than one ordinary family term. Do not repurpose the ID silently.

findings.reason: Normal when describing one’s own family; address forms and references to another person’s family differ. Avoid blanket replacement.

findings.suggestion: Keep 米 for uncooked rice; cooked rice requires ご飯.
findings.reason: The bare English rice prompt does not specify cooked versus uncooked. Decide the intended sense before editing.

findings.suggestion: Keep the object/liquid sense; weather uses 暑い.
findings.reason: The current adjective is normal for temperature of objects/liquids. An isolated English prompt does not establish weather versus object sense.

findings.suggestion: Keep the object/liquid sense; weather uses 寒い.
findings.reason: The current adjective is normal for temperature of objects/liquids. An isolated English prompt does not establish weather versus object sense.

findings.suggestion: Label dictionary you; teach name/omission use through appropriate context.
findings.reason: あなた is a dictionary equivalent, not a universal polite way to address strangers. Do not substitute another pronoun blindly.

findings.suggestion: Specify bell/green pepper, not pepper seasoning.
findings.reason: ピーマン fits the vegetable block. The bare English pepper is broader; context is the issue, not an unusual Japanese word.

findings.suggestion: Keep warm neck scarf as the intended sense.
findings.reason: マフラー does not cover every decorative scarf; preserve the intended useful winter object.

findings.suggestion: Keep bathing room as the intended sense; use トイレ for a toilet/restroom scenario.
findings.reason: English bathroom also means toilet/restroom, so an isolated label can mislead.

findings.suggestion: Consider 聞く for an everyday listen example, coordinated with the hear concept and distractors.
findings.reason: 耳を傾ける is valid but more elaborate than a typical first beginner listen expression. 聞く also covers hear; a mechanical substitution could create ambiguity. Editorial preference needs human review.

findings.suggestion: Consider 見る with a concrete looking context; review all see/watch/look choices together.
findings.reason: 目を向ける is valid but more elaborate than a common beginner default. Simpler alternatives overlap neighbouring visual verbs, so no isolated substitution is authorized.

findings.suggestion: Consider あげる in an explicit interpersonal giving example; decide participant relations first.
findings.reason: 与える is valid but often less natural for everyday interpersonal beginner examples. Japanese giving/receiving depends on relations; no universal replacement is proposed.

notes: Unflagged items are working keep decisions, not native certification or measured frequency rankings.
Source-supported findings retain the original full-text versus search-excerpt distinction in the reason; other recommendations are editorial.
Do not replace general train 列車 with electric train 電車 solely because another course uses it; 零 and ゼロ are legitimate context-dependent forms.
